extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in media studies, political economy of the media, and media bias
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating media bias with propaganda model
extracted.subtask_description: Use Herman and Chomsky's propaganda model to analyze or evaluate how mass-media reporting may be systematically distorted by institutional, economic, and ideological forces. The model identifies specific filters that shape news content and access to sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size, ownership, and profit orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: The dominant mass-media are large profit-based operations, and therefore they must cater to the financial interests of the owners such as corporations and controlling investors. The size of a media company is a consequence of the investment capital required for the mass-communications technology required to reach a mass audience of viewers, listeners, and readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As large, investor-owned enterprises, media organizations structure editorial choices to protect owners' financial interests; scale and capital requirements constrain who can participate in mass media and shape news priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: The advertising license to do business
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the majority of the revenue of major media outlets derives from advertising (not from sales or subscriptions), advertisers have acquired a 'de facto licensing authority.' Media outlets are not commercially viable without the support of advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News media must cater to the political prejudices and economic desires of their advertisers. This financial dependence weakens outlets oriented to working-class interests and helps explain attrition in the number of newspapers; editorial content is constrained to avoid alienating advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing mass media news
rubrics_metrics.description: Large bureaucracies of the powerful subsidize the mass media and gain special access by contributing to reducing the media's costs of acquiring and producing news. These large entities become 'routine' news sources and have privileged access to the gates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence on private and governmental sources privileges routine, official sources and marginalizes non-routine voices. If a news organization falls into disfavor with these sources it risks exclusion from information, loss of audience, and ultimately advertiser revenue, creating incentive to editorially favor government and corporate policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flak and the enforcers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Flak' refers to negative responses to a media statement or program (e.g. letters, complaints, lawsuits, or legislative actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flak can be costly in lost advertising revenue, legal defense, or reputational damage. Organized flak from powerful private influence groups (e.g., think tanks) acts as a deterrent to reporting certain facts or opinions and thereby shapes editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-communism (ideological control)
rubrics_metrics.description: This filter concerns the spectre of a common enemy which can be used to marginalise dissent: 'This ideology helps mobilize the populace against an enemy, and because the concept is fuzzy it can be used against anybody advocating policies that threaten [dominant] interests'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally focused on anti-communism as a control mechanism in the Cold War era, the model notes that such ideological frameworks can be repurposed (e.g., the 'war on terror') to delegitimize dissent and shape acceptable discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda model of communication (overall framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propaganda model describes five editorially distorting filters which are said to affect reporting of news in mass communications media, and situates media organizations within a tiered diagram of societal pillars (public domain, business firms, media organizations, governments) to explain dependencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the model as a holistic framework: examine how ownership, advertising revenue, sourcing patterns, flak, and dominant ideological paradigms jointly produce systematic biases. The model emphasizes media dependence on financial and institutional power and can be applied to analyze contemporary shifts (e.g., post–Cold War changes, effects of the internet).
